'''Dmitry Semionovitch Mirimanoff''' ({{langx|ru|Дми́трий Семёнович Мирима́нов}}; 13 September 1861, [[Pereslavl-Zalessky]], [[Russian Empire|Russia]] &ndash; 5 January 1945, [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]]) was a member of the [[Moscow Mathematical Society]] in 1897.<ref name="MathSoc">{{cite journal |year=1922 |title=Состав Математического Общества |url=http://mi.mathnet.ru/msb6920 |journal=Математический Сборник |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=1–3}}</ref> And later became a doctor of [[mathematical sciences]] in 1900, in Geneva, and taught at the universities of [[University of Geneva|Geneva]] and [[University of Lausanne|Lausanne]].

Mirimanoff made notable contributions to [[axiomatic set theory]] and to number theory (relating specifically to [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], on which he corresponded with [[Albert Einstein]] before the [[World War I|First World War]]<ref name="MirimanoffLokhmotov">Jean A. Mirimanoff.  Private correspondence with Anton Lokhmotov.  (2009)</ref>). In 1917, he introduced, though not as explicitly as [[John von Neumann]] later, the [[cumulative hierarchy]] of sets and the notion of [[ordinal number#Von Neumann definition of ordinals|von Neumann ordinals]]; although he introduced a notion of regular (and [[well-founded set]]) he did not consider [[axiom of regularity|regularity as an axiom]], but also explored what is now called [[non-well-founded set theory]] and had an emergent idea of what is now called [[bisimulation]].<ref name="SangiorgiRutten2011">{{cite book|editor=Davide Sangiorgi and Jan Rutten|title=Advanced Topics in Bisimulation and Coinduction|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8TScPLWJPnMC&pg=PA18|year=2011|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-00497-9|pages=18–19|chapter=Origins of bisimulation and coinduction|author=Davide Sangiorgi}}</ref><ref name="Halbeisen2011">{{cite book|author=Lorenz J. Halbeisen|title=Combinatorial Set Theory: With a Gentle Introduction to Forcing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NZVb54INnywC&pg=PA62|year=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4471-2172-5|pages=62–63}}</ref>

==Life==

Dmitry Semionovitch was born in [[Pereslavl-Zalessky]], [[Russian Empire|Russia]], on 13 September 1861. His parents were Semion Mirimanovitch Mirimanoff ({{langx|ru| Семён Мирима́нович Мирима́нов}}) and Maria Dmitrievna Rudakova ({{langx|ru| Мари́я Дми́триевна Рудакова}}).

Around 1885, Dmitry Mirimanoff met a [[French people|French]] woman, Malvina Geneviève Valentine Adriansen in [[Nice]]. Geneviève Adriansen learnt [[Russian language|Russian]] and accepted [[Russian Orthodox Church|Russian Orthodox Christianity]]. They married in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]] on 25 October 1897 and had two sons: Alexander (later Alexandre) Dmitrievitch Mirimanoff ({{langx|ru| Алекса́ндр Дми́триевич Мирима́нов}}), born in Oranienbaum (now [[Lomonosov, Russia|Lomonossov]]) in 1898, and Andreï (later André) Dmitrievitch Mirimanoff ({{langx|ru| Андрей Дми́триевич Мирима́нов}}), born in Geneva in 1902.

The family lived in [[Russian Empire|Russia]] (first, in [[Moscow]], then in [[Saint Petersburg|St Petersburg]]) until 1900 when they moved to Geneva (in search of a better climate for Dmitry Mirimanoff's bad health). After the [[Russian Revolution|1917 revolutions]] they never visited Russia, although Dmitry's sisters Sophia and Lydia remained there. Dmitry Mirimanoff became a [[Swiss citizen]] on 17 September 1926. He later died on 5 January 1945 in Geneva.

==Work==

===Set theory===
Mirimanoff in a 1917 paper introduced the concept of well-founded set and the notion of rank of a set.<ref>cf. {{cite book|author=Azriel Levy|title=Basic Set Theory|year=2002|publisher=Dover Publications|isbn=978-0-486-42079-0|page=68}} and {{cite book|author=Michael Hallett|title=Cantorian Set Theory and Limitation of Size|url=https://archive.org/details/cantoriansettheo00hall_545|url-access=limited|year=1996|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-853283-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/cantoriansettheo00hall_545/page/n208 186], 188}}</ref> Mirimanoff called a set ''x'' "regular" (French: "ordinaire") if every descending chain ''x'' ∋ ''x<sub>1</sub>'' ∋ ''x<sub>2</sub>''  ∋ ... is finite. Mirimanoff however did not consider his notion of regularity (well-foundedness) as an axiom to be observed by all sets;<ref name="Halbeisen2011"/> in later papers Mirimanoff also explored what are now called [[non-well-founded set theory|non-well-founded sets]] ("extraordinaire" in Mirimanoff's terminology).<ref name="SangiorgiRutten2011"/>

===Reflection method===

In 2008, [http://webspace.ship.edu/msrenault/ Marc Renault] published an article<ref Name="ReflectionPrinciple">{{cite journal|last = Renault|first = Marc| title = Lost (and Found) in Translation: André's ''Actual'' Method and Its Application to the Generalized Ballot Problem|journal = American Mathematical Monthly|volume = 115|number = 4|date = April 2008|pages = 358–362|url = http://webspace.ship.edu/msrenault/ballotproblem/monthly358-363-renault.pdf|jstor=27642480|doi = 10.1080/00029890.2008.11920537| s2cid=8126326 }}</ref> in which he pointed out that it is Dmitry Mirimanoff who should be credited for creating "[[Bertrand's ballot theorem#The reflection method|the reflection method]]" for solving [[Bertrand's ballot theorem|Bertrand's ballot problem]], not [[Désiré André]] to whom it had been long credited. Therefore, [[Donald Knuth]], who has read Renault's article, will credit Mirimanoff instead of André in future printings of Volume 1 of his monograph [[The Art of Computer Programming]].<ref name="KnuthLokhmotov">Donald E. Knuth. Private correspondence with Anton Lokhmotov. (2009)</ref>
